newsitem.title: UK: Backers stick up for Easdaq despite slow start.
newsitem.headline: Backers stick up for Easdaq despite slow start.

text.p: Backers of the fledgling Easdaq European growth stock market admitted on Wednesday it had got off to a slow start but said they were confident it would attract growing interest.
Once market-makers and investors started to work together, the market would have a good chance, they told a news conference.

Andrew Beeson, of London brokers Beeson Gregory, said Easdaq's timing had been dogged by what he saw as a downturn in the number of companies seeking a stock market listing. "It has done well with that in mind," he said.
So far the market, which started trading on November 27, has eight listings, with eight more in the works.
With its concentration on high-tech companies, it is aiming for a potentially profitable but volatile sector.

Competition with new, national markets such as London's Alternative Investment Market would make progress a little slow, said Joshua Rafner, managing director of international investment banking at U.S. investment bank Hambrecht and Quist.
"It is too early to see if there will be more pan-European investment," Rafner said. "We are developing a new market and there has to be a beginning."
He said there were "a lot of doubters" when NASDAQ -- the U.S. market on which Easdaq is modelled -- started out, too.
"It is not a surprise that it takes a little while for people to establish trust and communication," he added.
Beeson, a member of Easdaq's board, said interest from private investors would help. "I am encouraged by the fact that there is demand for issues out there, even from private investors," he said.
Entrepreneurs could especially benefit from Easdaq, Beeson added. "Easdaq does offer opportunities for larger entrepreneurial companies that normally would go to local exchanges," he said.
"It is also important...to go for a global perspective."
Dan Case, President and Chief Executive Officer of Hambrecht and Quist, agreed. "Our call here would be to entrepreneurs in the financial institutions," he said.
Those who got in early stood to make the most, he said. "There is no money in looking in the rear-view mirror," he added.
